In 2010 myself and my husband had the pleasure of visiting the beautiful state of Montana. We had friends out there, and stayed with them for the duration of our trip.

There are three things that I love about Montana:

[The open roads.](http://imgur.com/3nBd51E)

The kind, hippyish people.

And, of course, the natural beauty.

We first stayed in Missoula, which is surrounded by mountains. It is like most other cities - except it is more self contained, because the nearest large city is a few hours away. Whereas in NJ (where I live) we might have a hospital one town over, Missoula has everything that it needs.

But this post is not about Missoula. It's about our trip the Glacier National Park.

Glacier National Park is, without a doubt, the most beautiful place I've ever been to. With [waterfalls](http://imgur.com/FI5gNKj) and[ the glorious Rocky Mountains](http://i.imgur.com/mZr236w.jpg), one can't help but feel like you're on some sort of sacred ground. God's country.

We arrived on 02 July and set up in a [KoA cabin](http://imgur.com/UgH3B8N). Our friends took the one next door to us. There were several of these small cabins around, and we shared a communal washroom (it was like a fancy portapotty that had a shower).

On our second day there, we decided to take a hike. Our friends had described the beautiful glacier lakes that lay atop the mountains - only a 6 mile trek up. We decided to go for it.

It had rained earlier in the day, so when we started at the bottom, we saw numerous [rainbows](http://imgur.com/wrppJDB). And, though it was July, the temperature was around 70 degrees F - much colder than it was in our home state.

We trekked for three miles, and stopped. The higher we went, the colder it got, yet the [views were stunning.](http://imgur.com/OZ9N9V6) We sat near another waterfall and ate our lunch. When we finished, we resumed our hike.

This was my first "real" hike into true mountains, and I was ill equipped. I wore shorts, sneakers and a hoodie. Little did I know how cold it would get when we finally reached the top.

Because we were walking up-hill, the climb took longer than it would normally take someone to walk 6 miles. It took about three hours.

The last mile consisted of about a foot of snow. I was stunned. I shouldn't have been, but I was. It was July! And here I was, trying my best to walk through a foot of snow in shorts and soaked sneakers to get to our destination.

So, shivering and tired, I made my way up.

And I'm glad I did. When we arrived, we were greeted by the sight of a [clear, perfectly blue glacier lake](http://i.imgur.com/Yvf8azc.jpg).

We slowly made our way to its shoreline and stared in awe at it. Not a word was spoken. Our friends, who had seen it before, found it amusing how amazed we were.

After a bit, we decided to make our way back down. About 2.5 hours later, we arrived at our cabins, legs sore and tired.

The next day, I could hardly walk. My legs ached terribly. But it was worth it. I doubt I'll ever see anything quite so beautiful again.

NOTE: All credit for photographs goes to my husband.
